en: NAK 1-1697 11/7 *bauddhatantra* = NGMPP A 994/7 (palm-leaf, hook-topped): Fragment of a *Cakrasaṃvarasādhana* by a disciple of Ratnākaraśānti (most likely Śūnyasamādhivajra/Divākaracandra).
NB: *utpannakrama* → *Jñānodayatantra*!
Numerous parallels with the *Bhramahara* and the *Bhugmalokeśvarasādhana*—Péter-Dániel Szántó.

One who has well-grasped the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), whose sole refuge is the Three Jewels, who possesses faith, who has received all the initiations, who has long served at the feet of the excellent Guru, who has obtained permission, who possesses devotion inseparable from the Guru and Heruka, and who is wise— such a mantra-practitioner, having risen in the morning, should visualize within his own heart either a lunar disk transformed from the foremost of syllables or a solar disk, upon which is the syllable *HŪṂ*, resembling a great sapphire, radiant and having the nature of the three gates of liberation; having visualized this, he should perform the purification of the mouth and other parts.

Thereafter, having performed the protection of the place, oneself, and the yoga by means of the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should enter the meditation-chamber—which is smeared with fragrance and strewn with fragrant flowers—sit upon a soft seat, smear the mandala with the liquid of nectar, and scatter it with fragrant flowers.

Then, if possible, having placed an image of the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka on a cloth or similar support before oneself and having worshipped him with the five offerings, one should purify the water for the *argha* and other rites—which is contained in a vessel such as a conch shell made of ivory or the like and filled with fragrant flowers and nectar—before [the deity] according to the oral instructions. Having empowered it seven times with the mantra of one's own heart interlaced (*vidarbhitena*) with the three syllables, one should duly place the receiving vessel before it.
If, however, this is not possible, one should perform all of that through meditative resolve (*adhimucya*).
[This is done] with the mantra of one's own heart.

Then, having visualized all the Tathāgatas together with their hosts of Bodhisattvas—drawn forth by the hook-like rays of light from the mantra in one's own heart—situated in the space before one in the ten directions, one should worship them with the outer and secret offerings by means of the offering goddesses emerging from the mouths of the rays of light of the mantra in one's own heart.
Then, imagining oneself before them with body bowed in prostration and hands joined in *añjali*, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth, [reciting]:
"In the successions of cyclic existences, which are filled with delusion, [I have committed] sin..."
Whatever [evil] has been accumulated by my body, speech, and mind that brings about calamity,
I confess it all in its entirety, bowing down in great fear before the Victors, whose minds are overwhelmed with compassion.

Having rejoiced in all the pure and supreme merit that was performed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the Sons of the Buddha, those born of the Buddha-family, and others, may I, with well-born joy, [dedicate it].
I dedicate [this] to enlightenment, the treasury of great qualities.
Until I reach enlightenment, I go for refuge to the One Possessing the Ten Powers,
who has utterly destroyed the mass of faults and whose mind is moistened with compassion.
The pure Dharma, this vast vehicle, the entire Saṅgha, and the great assembly of the Sons of the Conquerors who possess virtuous qualities.
I secretly offer this body of mine to the Buddha, who is compassionate toward his assembly of disciples,
so that it may be employed for his own desired purpose.
Let him make an effort to take possession of her immediately.
Oh, may I indeed attain the most excellent, unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world,
[and follow] the unsurpassed path to enlightenment that grants great benefit!
I take refuge in this most secret vehicle.

Then, for the sake of providing no opportunity for ill-will, harmfulness, delight, or sensual passion; for the sake of supporting all roots of virtue beginning with the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); and for the sake of protecting oneself from suffering, miserable rebirths, Māra, and the Lesser Vehicle, one should take hold of all suffering sentient beings and cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward them in the form of bestowing divine happiness. Next, one should cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those very same beings in the form of removing all their suffering. Finally, one should cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward those very same beings in the form of establishing them in the happiness already bestowed, lasting as long as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) endures.

Upon those very [objects], one should cultivate equanimity characterized by the gathering of all mundane and supramundane wholesome factors for the sake of exhausting all unwholesome factors, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*). This is the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*).
% °kṣayāya [3v] laukika°

Then, for the sake of the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*), one should generate a mind that is free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*). That which appears as an error in the form of blue, yellow, and so forth—just like a dream—is this very mind itself. For there is nothing to be grasped by the mind that exists external to the mind. Furthermore, that mind is not a grasper (*grāhaka*), because in the absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*), the grasper cannot exist. Therefore, all phenomena have the mind as their essence. Their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the emptiness of duality.

Having thus determined with absolute certainty, one should abandon the forms of all phenomena—which are the causes of delusion and superimposed by delusion—and perceive only the nature of all phenomena itself: characterized as non-dual cognition, resembling pure crystal, like the sky at midday in autumn, infinite, and the very essence of all things. This is that ultimate *bodhicitta*, the cause for the accomplishment of the purification of the meditative cultivation of the meaning of all mantras.

This very supramundane gnosis of emptiness is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*). This is that primary *prajñāpāramitā*. This alone is the supreme protection. Having meditated upon that, one should consecrate it with this mantra: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-gnosis of emptiness. [Pure by nature...]

Then, one should meditate upon the protective enclosure (*rakṣā*) which is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of that [meditative concentration], possessing form and having the nature of pure mundane gnosis (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*). Therein, from the rays of the mantra at one's own heart, one should emanate Sumbharājas in the form of Heruka, with four faces and four arms, embracing their respective consorts (*svābhavidyā*) with both primary hands, while holding a vajra-hammer (*vajramudgara*) and a vajra-stake (*vajrakīla*) in the second right and left hands respectively; having emanated them, one should station them in the directions starting with the east by reciting each individual mantra.

Therein, one should station [the deity] in the eastern direction with "Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ 2 phaṭ"; in the northern direction with "Oṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ"; in the western direction with "Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ"; and in the southern direction with "Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vajrarāja hūṃ 2 phaṭ."

There, one should urge them with this mantra: *Oṃ gha gha ghātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭavighnān hūṃ phaṭ; oṃ kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān hūṃ 2 phaṭ; oṃ hūṃ 3 vajrakīla vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvaduṣṭavighnānāṃ kāyavākcittavajrān kīlaya 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ*. Then, one should visualize that those [kīlas], thus urged, are driven into the heads of the obstructors situated in all directions.
Then, with the mantra *oṃ vajramudgara vajrakīlākoṭaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should visualize those Lords of Wrath being dispatched and driving in the vajra-kila pegs with vajra-hammers.

Thereafter, having visualized in front [of oneself] a vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*, which is blue, with its tip pointing upward, and blazing intensely, one should emanate from it a web of subtle vajras flaming with garlands of rays. From these, which have become extremely dense and are situated in the four directions, a square vajra-fortress (*vajraprākāra*) is constructed; above, by those [rays] reaching upward, a vajra-canopy (*vajrapañjara*) and a net of arrows (*śarajāla*); below, by those reaching downward, a ground made of vajra extending down to the subterranean realm of *Ārasātala*. Furthermore, from the vajra-canopy and the other [structures], rays of light radiate in every direction.

Having visualized a wall of vajra-fire flames outside and far away from the solidification [of the mandala], and having also visualized a canopy of vajras formed by rays of light ascending from the *hūṃ*-vajra, one should consecrate everything with the mantras. Here is the mantra-phrase:

Oṃ vajraprākāra hūṃ vaṃ hūṃ; oṃ vajrapañjara hūṃ paṃ hūṃ; oṃ śarajāla trāṃ śaṃ bhrūṃ; oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ; oṃ vajrajvālānalārka hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ; oṃ vajravitāna hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ. Thus is the twofold procedure for protection (*rakṣāvidhāna*). According to the opinion of some, however, the rite of protection is accomplished by the mere recitation of the mantras.
Then, in this manner...

Then, having resolved upon the absolute non-existence of obstacles, one should visualize the element of space as white as the autumnal moon—subtle below and broad above, triangular in shape, with the nature of the inner sky, possessing the essence of Mahāvajradhara, and known as the *dharmodayā*. Within its womb, one should contemplate the eight cremation grounds, which indicate the selflessness of all world-realms and are crowded with hosts of *śiva*, *vetāla*, *bhūta*, and other spirits.

There, in the eastern direction is the cremation ground named Caṇḍogra, consisting of a mass of burnt wood; in the north is Gahvara, a mass of broken wood; in the west is Jvālakaraṅka, a mass of discarded wood; in the south is Vibhīṣaṇa, a mass of impaled bodies on spikes, known as Aṭṭahāsa; in the northeast is Ekasthāna, a mass of half-burnt wood; in the southeast is Kiṅkiṇīka, a mass of suspended corpses; in the southwest is Ghora, a mass of those buried in pits; and in the northwest is the cremation ground named Jvālāviddha, a mass of unbroken wood.
[One should visualize] the Pāṭala, Sāla, Yajñāṅga, Pippala, and Puṇḍarīka trees.
One should visualize a *nāga* tree, a *vaṭa* tree, and a *śirīṣa* tree there.
One should contemplate eight [beings] with the faces of a crow, Indra, a horse, a *kola*, a cat, a *preta*, a vulture, and a tiger upon these trees. (The first is) the crow-Indra.
Surrounded by crows, owls, dogs, jackals, hyenas, vultures, eagles, and *tarakṣu* beasts,
as well as by young students (*baṭu*), they stood there in their preeminent state.

Then, one should visualize the guardians of the directions together with their wives at the roots of the trees. Therein, one should visualize Indra as yellow in color, thousand-eyed, wearing a jewel crown, holding a vajra, adorned with divine garments and ornaments, mounted upon the white elephant Airāvata, and surrounded by hosts of gods. One should visualize Dhanada (Kubera) as golden-colored, wearing a jewel crown, holding a goad and a mace, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, and surrounded by hosts of yakṣas. One should visualize Varuṇa as white in color, having seven hoods, holding a serpent-noose and a conch, mounted upon a makara, and surrounded by hosts of nāgas. One should visualize Yama as black in color...

[One should visualize] Raktākṣa, who has brown eyebrows and hair standing erect, carries a staff and a trident, rides a buffalo, and is surrounded by hosts of *preta*s; Īśāna, who is white in color, wears a crown of matted locks, has the moon as his crest-jewel, possesses three eyes, is adorned with a garland of skulls, has four arms, holds a fire-vessel (*kṛpīṭa*), a skull-cup, a trident, and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, rides a bull, and is surrounded by hosts of spirits (*bhūta*s); and Agni, who is red in color, wears a crown of matted locks and a sacred thread, has four arms, holds a rosary, a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*), and a wooden staff, rides a goat, and is surrounded by hosts of sages.

One should visualize Nirṛti as blue in color, with tawny hair standing erect and bound in a crown of matted locks, adorned with a garland of skulls, holding a small knife and a skull-cup in his hands, mounted upon a corpse, and surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas. One should likewise visualize Vāyu as smoke-colored, wearing a cloth fluttering in the wind, adorned with a jewel crown, mounted upon a deer, and surrounded by a host of Maruts and a multitude of sages.

Then, on their left sides, one should visualize eight nāga kings with hoods: there, Vāsuki, resembling the moon, with his head marked by a blue lotus; Takṣaka, resembling a bandhūka flower, with his head marked by a svastika; Karkoṭa, dark green like dūrvā grass, with his neck marked by three lines; Padma, as white as a conch shell, with his hood marked by a śrīvatsa; Mahāpadma, with the luster of a jasmine flower, marked by a trident; Huluhulu, resembling crushed collyrium, with his head marked by a lotus; and Kulika, smoke-colored.

One should visualize [the deity] with a throat marked by a crescent moon, holding a conch, golden in color, and with a throat adorned by the mark of a crescent moon. On his back, one should contemplate clouds: there, one should contemplate the *garjita* cloud as black in color, the *ghūrṇita* as multicolored (*viśvavarṇa*), the *ghora* as saffron-colored, the *āvarta* as blue, the *ghana* as white, the *pūraṇa* as yellow, the *varṣaṇa* as grey, and the *caṇḍa* as the color of collyrium.
Alternatively, one may also release the aforementioned charnel grounds and so forth, as well as jackals, vetālas, and the like.

Alternatively, one should visualize within that [space], situated therein, the four great elements in the form of four mandalas, having the nature of the four goddesses, arranged one above the other. First, one should see a deep blue [mandala] arising from the syllable *yaṃ*, shaped like a bow, marked with a fluttering banner, and filled with smoke. Above that, one should meditate on the fire-mandala arising from the syllable *raṃ*; it is triangular, marked with the letter *ra* at its corners and with a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and is intensely radiant, filled with flames.

Above that, one should visualize the pure Varuṇa-maṇḍala, which arises from the syllable *vaṃ*, circular, marked with a vase, resembling the moon, and accompanied by rays of light. Above that, one should behold the Mahendra-maṇḍala, arising from the syllable *laṃ*, square, with its corners marked by vajras.
Then, one should contemplate Sumeru, the abode of great liberation, which is the condensed form of the completely purified Buddha-field.
Therein [is] that which arises from the syllable *suṃ*, square and elevated.
Divine, consisting of the four jewels, and adorned with eight peaks.
One should visualize Mount Meru, strewn with trees of gold and jewels, the abode of hosts of bodhisattvas, illuminating the entire realm with its radiance.

Then, upon its back, on a pedestal of a triple-pronged universal vajra produced from the syllable *hūṃ* situated in the pericarp of a universal eight-petaled lotus, there is a moon disc formed by the white vowels beginning with *a*, which are the nature of wisdom; this has the nature of the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*). Above that is a sun disc formed by the red consonants beginning with *ka*, which are the nature of skillful means; this has the nature of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*). In the center of that—

One should visualize a five-pronged vajra transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ* and containing the syllable *HŪṂ* at its core, whose intrinsic nature is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). From the rays of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one emanates all the Tathāgatas in the form of the circle of heroes and heroines; having withdrawn them back in that same manner, one contemplates the syllable *HŪṂ*—which has become unified with them—as being the intrinsic nature of the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Then, arising from the transformation of the moon, sun, vajra, and seed-syllable, there appears a nine-pointed thunderbolt (*kuliśa*) with a central hub empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the intrinsic nature of the glorious Vajrasattva.
One should meditate on that which has the nature of emanation and reabsorption, whose essence is the wisdom of the utterly pure dharmadhātu.
This "three-pronged [vajra] produced from it" consists of five aspects; this is the gentle yoga.

Then, through the yoga of emanation from the syllable *hūṃ*, having visualized the universe as consisting of infinite Tathāgatas in the form of the circle of heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*), and as dependent upon the mind; and through the yoga of reabsorption, having fully understood all that to be like an illusion and like space, one should meditate on oneself as the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka, born from the transformation of the vajra-seed.
He is like an illusion, with the luster of crushed collyrium and sapphire, four-armed and four-faced.
His faces are black, dark, reddish, and golden, and he has twelve eyes.
Endowed with twelve arms and standing in the *ālīḍha* posture,
he performs the *tāṇḍava* dance upon the seat formed by the breasts and foreheads of Raudrī and Rudra.
Having performed an embrace with Vārāhī, he holds a skull-topped staff and a bell with his two primary hands,
wears an elephant hide as a garment, and carries [other implements] with his two remaining arms.
In the third right hand he holds a ḍamaru, in the fourth a blazing axe,
in the fifth a curved knife, and in the sixth an uplifted trident.
In the third left hand is a khaṭvāṅga adorned with a banner and small bells;
its upper, lower, and middle parts are marked with a five-pronged vajra, like a double-vajra (viśvavajra).
In the fourth [hand] he holds a skull-bowl filled with blood; in the fifth, a vajra-noose;
and in the sixth, a bleeding Brahma-head, while possessing four faces.
Adorned with a crown of matted hair marked by a half-moon and a skull,
his head is emblazoned with a double-vajra, and his crest is a garland of skulls.
With prominent fangs, most terrifying, and endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments;
possessing stout limbs, in the prime of youth, and with round, blood-red eyes.
His face radiates the syllable *hūṃ*,
possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns;
he wears a necklace of blood-dripping severed heads and threatens the gods and asuras.
Wearing the sacred thread, wrathful, adorned with the five mudrās,
clothed in a tiger-skin garment, and his body smeared with ashes.
Then one should meditate upon Vajravārāhī, who resembles a *kiṃśuka* flower,
having two arms, one face, three eyes, and loose, disheveled hair.
Naked, with a beautiful form, adorned with a fragment of a girdle,
possessing the fiery luster of fierce eyes, with blood flowing from her mouth, she was most excellent.
Holding in her left hand a skull-cup filled with blood,
and in her right hand she bears a vajra that brings an end to the wicked.
Enveloping him with both her legs and raising herself to embrace him with her two arms, she kisses Heruka, her beloved; full of bliss, she is fond of blood.
Some say that one should meditate on the Blessed One as the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ* born from the union of *āli* and *kāli*.

Others say he is the transformation of Vajrasattva upon the seat within the interior of a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) surrounded by the eight cremation grounds situated on the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Such is the Anuyoga.

Then, having visualized the syllable *hūṃ* in the sun at the heart, one should contemplate the syllable *vaṃ* in the moon at the heart of the Goddess. Thereafter, one should generate the mind of the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of the five aggregates (*skandhas*). In that regard, within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is white Vairocana, transformed from the syllable *oṃ*; in the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) is yellow Vajrasūrya, transformed from the syllable *ā*; in the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) is red Padmanarteśvara, born from the syllable *hrīḥ*; in the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is green Vajrarāja, born from the syllable *hoḥ*; and in the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is [the deity] white, arisen from the syllable *hūṃ*.
One should visualize Vajrasattva as the Śrī Heruka-vajra, black in color and transformed from the syllable *hrīḥ*, abiding within the state of all Tathāgatas.
Upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*),
there is a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, and a double-vajra, all blazing with light.
Holding a heart-vajra, touch, and a mudrā with her right hands.
Holding bells in their left hands, they are three-eyed and stand upon a corpse atop a universal lotus, moon, and sun mandala.

Then, one should generate the mind of ego-identification with the sense bases (*āyatana*) as follows: one should resolve that in the two eyes there is white Delusion-Vajra, born from the syllable *bhrūṃ*; in the two ears, black Hatred-Vajra, transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*; in the nose, yellow Envy-Vajra, born from the syllable *khaṃ*; in the mouth, red Passion-Vajra, born from the syllable *ā*; in the [body] of touch, green Avarice-Vajra, born from the syllable *hā*; and in all the sense bases, white Sovereignty-Vajra, born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Furthermore, these possess the characteristics described for the ego-identification of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Then, one should visualize: in the earth element, the yellow Pātanī born from the syllable *lāṃ*; in the water element, the black Māraṇī born from the syllable *māṃ*; in the fire element, the gold-colored Ākarṣaṇī born from the syllable *yāṃ*; in the wind element, the red Padmanarteśvarī born from the syllable *tāṃ*; and in the space element, the playful blue Padmajvālinī born from the syllable *khaṃ*.

Furthermore, these [deities], situated in their respective maṇḍalas, each have one face and four arms. With their first right hands they hold a wheel, a thunderbolt, a lotus, and a sword; with their second [right hands] a flaying knife (*kartṛ*). With their first left hands they hold skull-cups (*kapāla*), and with their second left hands they hold *khaṭvāṅgas*. Padmajvālinī, however, has six arms and three faces; she holds a goad, a Brahma-head, and a flaying knife in her right hands, and she holds a skull-cup, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a noose in her left hands. Alternatively, one should visualize the seed-syllables themselves as the colors of the deities upon the shoulders and other parts. In the fire element, [one visualizes] the goddess born from the syllable *YĀM*.

Having thus resolved upon the purity of the deities of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, one should resolve upon the heroes, adorned with ornaments and signs as will be described, within those very same sense-bases: Khaṇḍakapālin in the nails and teeth; Mahākaṅkāla in the hair of the head and body; Kaṅkāla in the skin and impurities; Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin in the flesh; Surāvairin in the sinews; Amitābha in the bones; Vajraprabha in the kidneys; Vajradeha in the heart; Aṅkurika in the eyes; Vajrajaṭila in the bile; [and] in the lungs...

One should visualize Mahāvīra in the intestines, Vajrahūṃkāra in the entrails, Subhadra in the two tendons, Vajrabhadra in the belly, Mahābhairava in the feces, Virūpākṣa in the hairline, Mahābala in the phlegm, Ratnavajra in the pus, Hayagrīva in the blood, Ākāśagarbha in the sweat, Śrīheruka in the fat, Padmanarteśvara in the tears, Vairocana in the saliva, and Vajrasattva in the nasal mucus. [9v] Aṅkuśikā.

Then, one should meditate upon the *samayacakra*, which arises from the three syllables, having the nature of the previously mentioned eight-petaled lotus, mounted upon the *māhendra* mandala, multicolored, the unified form of the three wheels, presided over by the syllable *Śrīṃ*, encircled by a garland of jewels, consisting of the body of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and having the essence of mind, speech, and body. Therein, one should visualize the blue Ḍākinī on the eastern petal, the green Lāmā on the northern petal, the red Khaṇḍarohā on the western petal, and the yellow Rūpiṇī on the southern petal.
All of them, moreover, are mounted upon corpses and stand in the *ālīḍha* posture.
With disheveled hair, they are full of great bliss, possessing one face and four arms.
In their left hands they hold khaṭvāṅgas and skull-cups, eager for enchantment;
in their right hands they hold ḍamarus and flaying knives, flashing with radiant luster.
Three-eyed, naked, fierce, with faces made formidable by fangs;
three-eyed,
endowed with the sentiments of erotic love and the rest, and adorned with the five mudrās.
Then the yogi should visualize, for the purpose of worship, skull-cups of bodhicitta situated upon the vases at the intermediate corners.

Then, outside of that, one should visualize the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), born from the syllable *hūṃ*, having eight spokes, mounted upon the mandala of Varuṇa, black in color, presided over by the syllable *he*, surrounded by a garland of vajras, whose nature is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), whose form is heaven, and whose essence is the sky-farer (*khecarī*).

There, on his crown, one should visualize Pracaṇḍā embracing Khaṇḍakapālin at Pullīramalaya in the eastern spoke; Caṇḍākṣī embracing Mahākaṅkāla at Jālandhara in the northern spoke; Prabhāvatī embracing Kaṅkāla at Oḍḍiyāna in the western spoke; and Mahānāsā embracing Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin at Arbuda in the southern spoke. Thus, the sacred site (pīṭha) is the stage of Joy (pramuditā), the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā), and the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna).

In Goja, in the southeast at Godāvarī, one should meditate on Surāvairocana and Vīramatī; in Rāja, in the southwest at Rāmeśvara, Amitābha and Kharvarī; in Deja, in the northwest at Devikoṭṭa, Vajraprabha and Laṅkeśvarī; and in Māja, in the northeast at Mālava, Vajradeha and Drumacchāyā. Thus is the *upapīṭha*; it is the stage of Vimalā, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*). This is the mind. In Mālava is Vajradeha.

Then, outside of that, one should visualize the Speech Wheel (*vākcakra*), which is born from the syllable *ĀḤ*, possesses eight spokes, is mounted upon the Varuṇa-maṇḍala, presided over by the syllable *Ru*, is red in color, encircled by a garland of lotuses, consists of the Saṃbhoga-kāya, has the nature of a mortal, and takes the form of Bhūcarī. Therein, upon its petals: on the eastern petal in Kāmarūpa is Aṅkurika with Airāvatī; on the northern petal in Oḍra is Vajrajaṭila with Mahābhairavī; and on the western petal in Triśakuni is Mahāvīra with Vāyuvegā.

In the southern spoke of Kośalā is Vajrahūṃkāra with Surābhakṣī; this is the secondary field (upakṣetra), the Radiant Stage (arciṣmatī bhūmiḥ), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), and the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñāna). In Kaja, on the southeastern spoke of Kaliṅga, is Subhadra with Śyāmādevī; in Laṃja, on the southwestern spoke of Lampāka, is Vajrabhadra with Subhadrā; this is the chandoha, the Facing Stage (abhimukhī bhūmiḥ), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).

In Kāñcī, at the northwest corner, [one worships] Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā; in Himālaya, at the northeast corner, Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā. Thus is the Upacchandoha, the stage [bhūmi] that is very difficult to conquer, which is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the Knowledge of the Path (*mārgajñāna*).
[11–20] [End of section]. [With the possible exception of this next folio, ...]

Then, having emanated the goddesses of worship from the garland of light rays issuing from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and having filled the expanse of the sky with the clouds of their emanations, one should worship the Lord of the Mandala together with his retinue. Then, having resolved that all phenomena are like an illusion and similar to a dream, one should praise the Blessed One with two verses:
"O Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, excellent Saṃvara, Vajraḍāka, preeminent Hero among the sovereigns of heroes, Lord of the Gaṇas!"
I bow to your lotus feet, which are embraced by a pair of arms gracefully placed upon the necks of Kola and Anana, overflowing with compassion,
attainable through yoga alone, and the breaker of the bonds of worldly existence.
O you whose essence of body is expanded, increased, and utterly pure;
O you whose form is stainless awakening that has utterly destroyed faults and evils— I worship and bow to the pollen of your lotus feet.

Then, having visualized in the intermediate space the wind-maṇḍala—born from the syllable *yam*, black, resembling a bow, and marked with a fluttering banner—and above that the fire-maṇḍala—born from the syllable *ram*, triangular, marked with the letter *repha*, and red; and above that, resting upon three skulls, a white lotus-bowl born from the syllable *āḥ*, turned upward, within whose interior one should meditate upon the five nectars together with the five powers, sealed by the syllable *hūṃ*.

Then, the melting of that [substance] through heat produced by fire fanned by wind is the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*); its becoming of one flavor with the *vajra* is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*); the vision of the forms of all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions by means of the rays of the white *praṇava* syllable above it is the discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); the drawing in of those Tathāgatas, who consist of gnosis, by those very rays and their pouring into the nectar is the all-accomplishing gnosis (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*); and having become of one flavor with them, the transformation into supreme nectar is the gnosis of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*).

Having thus purified that [substance] with the five wisdoms and empowered it with the three syllables, one should visualize a white, radiant vajra on the tongue by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, and resolve upon a maṇḍala on the sun at the heart; with that, one should satisfy oneself and the maṇḍala, and utter: *oṃ samayaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ samayaśuddho ’ham*.
[This is] sealed by the recitation of the syllable *hūṃ*.

Then, with a concentrated mind, the practitioner [visualizes] within the womb of the union of the moon and sun, which have arisen from the transformation of the vowels and consonants in the *nirmāṇacakra*, the nature of Vajravārāhī—which is the essence of the *dharmadhātu*—arising from the transformation of the seed-syllable of nectar. He should worship it...

[21r] *Śraddhābalā* is Mahābhairavā; *Vīryabalā* is Vāyuvegā; *Smṛtibalā* is Surābhakṣī; *Samādhibalā* is Śyāmādevī; *Prajñābalā* is Subhadrā. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are those known as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity. Here, "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) refers to the realization of reality through mere vision; these are its limbs. Furthermore, the vision of this path is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), which is the body, while the remaining [factors] are the equipment.

For it is thus: through the establishment of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one attains the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), which consists in the vision of the truths; and by means of vigor (*vīrya*), one brings that discernment to completion without remainder. Furthermore, one obtains joy (*prīti*) in its accomplishment, and through pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), one is not withdrawn from abiding in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because by that [pliancy] the depravity (*dauṣṭhulya*) consisting of the seeds of the afflictions is removed. That [state] is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Thus, there are the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptasaṃbodhyaṅga*).

Therein, Hayakarṇā is the factor of awakening that is concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); Khagānanā is the factor of awakening that is vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Thus is the purification of the deities of the speech wheel. [Cakravegā is the factor of awakening that is joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); Khaṇḍarohā is the factor of awakening that is pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); Śauṇḍinī is the factor of awakening that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*); Cakravarmiṇī is the factor of awakening that is mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); [Suvīrā is the factor of awakening that is equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*); Right View, Intention, Speech, Action, Livelihood, Effort, Mindfulness, and Concentration are the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgika-mārga*). Among these, Right View is the body, while the remaining factors are the ornaments.

In that regard, the vision of the [Truths] through the instruction of a teacher is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Establishing them according to one's realization and teaching them accordingly is, in due order, right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*). Right speech and right action constitute the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*). Right livelihood consists in the seeking of robes and other requisites in accordance with the Dharma.

The right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*), right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) are, respectively, that vigor, mindfulness, and concentration by which one abandons without remainder the obscuration of the afflictions such as passion, the obscuration of the secondary afflictions such as lethargy, and the obscuration of qualities such as the superknowledges. Among them, right view is the Great Power (*Mahābalā*); right intention is the Universal Monarch (*Cakravartinī*); and right speech is the Great Heroine (*Mahāvīryā*). This is the purification of the deities of the body-wheel. The limb is *Śauṇḍinī*.
Right action is Kākāsyā; right livelihood is Ulūkāsyā; right effort is Śvānāsyā; right mindfulness is Sūkarāsyā; and right concentration is the Blessed One Śrī Heruka. Right livelihood...

Through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there is the thorough knowledge of defiled phenomena that consist of error and of purifying phenomena that consist of non-error; thereafter, the vigor for the arising of wholesome phenomena not yet arisen is Yamadāḍhī; the vigor for the maintenance of wholesome phenomena already arisen is Yamadūtī; the vigor for the abandonment of unwholesome phenomena already arisen is Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī; and the vigor for the non-arising of unwholesome phenomena not yet arisen is Yamamathanī. Thus is the purification of the deities of the gates and corners.
Thus, having recollected the purity of the deity through the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), one should resolve upon other purities as well:
Vajrasattva is the crown, or Akṣobhya due to the purity of gnosis (*jñāna*).
By means of the root mantra, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) is prepared for the heroes.
The necklace, the ornament for the neck, belongs to Vajravārāhī with her mantra;
the garland of fifty severed heads belongs to the Blessed One with his heart-mantra.
A garland of fifty skulls [is worn] with the seven-syllable mantra; an earring as an ear-ornament [is worn] with the *upahṛd* mantra of the Goddess; and a garment of elephant-hide is donned.
On the head, he should place a skull-crest with the Heart-mantra of the Goddess;
the girdle and waist-ornament with the mantra of the six Yoginīs.
With the mantras of the six heroes, one performs the six mudrās as ornaments for all the limbs;
the mantra of the goddesses situated on the wheel is that of a skull-cup filled with blood.
The elements within the body are considered to be the twenty-four heroes;
through the mantra of worshiping the Lord, one shall always maintain celibacy.
Immediately after that, one should make aspirational prayers for the sake of accomplishing the desired goal; briefly, by means of these three verses:
"May I attain the supreme, eternal state known as Heruka, and may I cause the entire world to attain it through this merit."
May I too always possess that practice by which unsurpassed enlightenment was attained by the Bodhisattvas, as I long for awakening at all times.
Just as the perfectly awakened ones conduct themselves for the sake of all sentient beings,
so shall I conduct myself, assuming the form of Śrī Heruka and the others.

Thereafter, having performed the worship, praise, and so forth as before, one should dissolve all the heroes and yoginīs into the seed-syllable in one’s own heart. Then, having resolved upon the extremely vast vajra-fence and so forth, one should visualize the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) dissolving into the element of space, the mandalas of wind and the others dissolving into the external elements of wind and so forth, and Mount Sumeru dissolving into the house and other surroundings; then, with the ego-identification of Heruka, one should arise.
Thereafter...

Even when risen from [meditation], one should dwell having resolved that one's own support—the body and so forth—is the nature of the mandala as the supported within the support. In this regard: "That which is this element of space is my *dharmodaya*; these external elements, such as wind and the rest, are my mandala of the four elements, whose intrinsic nature is the goddesses Narteśvarī and the others; this house and so forth is my abode of liberation, Sumeru; that which is my body is my chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), and I am the Lord of the Mandala.
Furthermore, one should apply the essence of the ego-identification with the aggregates and so forth in this manner.

During the intermediate juncture (*sandhyā*), having entered the abode of meditation and sat upon the seat, one should visualize the foundational mandala (*ādhāramaṇḍala*) manifested as the five elements. Within that, one should instantly manifest oneself as Śrī Heruka, seated upon the central throne with his neck embraced by Vārāhī. From the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one should emanate all the heroes and yoginīs and establish them in their respective places. Having resolved upon the purification of one’s own aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, and having meditated on everything as consisting of bliss, one should perform—as before—the consecration, worship, praise, tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), recitation (*japa*), and so on.

Having brought the ritual to its conclusion with the final vow (*praṇidhāna*) and likewise dissolved the maṇḍala, one should rise while maintaining the divine pride (*ahaṃkāra*) of Heruka. Even after rising, one should perform everything as before. The same applies to the evening twilight session; however, this is the distinction: *Oṃ!
You have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; you have bestowed the accomplishments according to [their] dispositions. Go to the realm of the Buddhas, so that you may return again.*
Having recited "Oṃ Vajra Mur" and offered the *argha* and other offerings, one should dismiss the *jñānamaṇḍala* and dissolve the *samayamaṇḍala* within oneself as before.

Furthermore, at the time of sleep, one should go to bed while bringing the yoga of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) to mind. At dawn, having resolved that one has awakened through the power of the impetus of previous aspirations, one should rise from sleep; having risen, one should perform everything as on the preceding day.

In this manner, one should perform all of this every day, at each junction of the day, or whenever the opportunity arises, until one perceives the signs of accomplishment (*siddhinimitta*). Furthermore, the signs of accomplishment are as follows: when the visualized maṇḍala becomes vivid through the continuous flow of effortless joy and absorption (*laya*), [then success is attained].
When there is no sensation from being struck by a whip, a slap, or the like, then accomplishment is not far off. [cf. Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi 2.8] From being struck by a whip, a slap, and so forth...
If the sharp sound of beaten drums and other instruments were not within the range of hearing,
would supreme, unsurpassed enlightenment still be attained?

For one who possesses meditative concentration, supreme accomplishment is attained quickly even in a dream. Having thus observed the signs of accomplishment, being composed and accompanied by a pure companion, one should employ the means through the yoga of the *utpannakrama* for the sake of great accomplishment.

For the sake of accomplishing one’s desired aims and pacifying obstacles, at all three junctions of the day, having purified [the area] according to the instruction and empowered it with the mantra, one should offer a bali-oblation to all beings. Therein, standing with the right foot advanced or in the *ālīḍha* posture, gazing upward and uttering the sound "phet," one should form the *jvālāmudrā*, place it at the region of the forehead, and rotate it in a circular motion.

Then, having visualized the guardians of all directions and other deities and so forth—drawn forward by the hooks of the garlands of light rays from the mantra of one’s own heart and standing before one—as purified in the form of heroic yoginīs, and having worshipped them with the five offerings preceded by the presentation of *argha* and the rest, one should recite the pledge-mantra (*samayamantra*): *oṃ vajrārali hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ vakraḍākinyas samayas tvaṃ hoḥ*. Thus twice and thrice as well.

Then one should apply the heart-mudrā with the left and right hands, rotating it in the manner of a lotus-turn (*kamalāvarta*), which brings true bliss to the network of *ḍākinīs*. Then, having visualized the syllable *HŪṂ* upon their tongues, one should offer the purified oblation (*bali*) held before them with an upward-opened vajra-gesture (*vajrāñjali*), while reciting the mantra:

Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi! May all yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, unmādas, apasmāras, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, and so forth, accept this *bali* offering; protect the *samaya*; grant me all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Eat, drink, and smell as you wish and according to your pleasure; do not transgress against me in any way. Be my helpers for the sake of purifying true bliss in every respect! Huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
At midnight, having become naked with hair disheveled, one should stand facing the southern direction and offer the *bali* at a high place.

Then, having recited the hundred-syllable mantra of the Vakraḍākinīs’ commitment (*samaya*), one should rise: *Oṃ vajraheruka, protect the commitment! Abide as Heruka! Be firm for me! Be well-pleased with me! Be well-nourished by me! Be devoted to me! Grant me all accomplishments! And in all activities, make my mind auspicious! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha ho! O Blessed One Vajraheruka, do not abandon me! Be Heruka for me! Great Being of the Commitment! Āḥ hūṃ phaṭ!* Ha ha ha ha.
This yoga of the generation stage is completed.

Here, the practitioner who is authorized, having accumulated the provisions and possessing the vidyā, desiring the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, free from unreal conceptualization, makes his dwelling in a mountain cave, on the shore of the great ocean, on the bank of a lake, at the root of a tree, in a temple of the Mothers, in a temple of Śiva, in a garden, in a cremation ground, at a crossroads, in a monastery, in a shrine, or in a house—any secluded, undisturbed, and favorable place. He reflects: "All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; I am empty of intrinsic nature. All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature."

Having ascertained that one's own body is indeed the mandala of the support and the supported, one should resolve upon it as follows: therein, one should resolve that the body hairs are the stakes, the skin is the vajra-fence, the skeletal frame is the vajra-cage, the network of veins is the net of arrows, the fluids and so forth are the vajra-canopy, and the flesh and so forth are the vajra-ground; then, one should resolve that the interior space is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).

Therein, by means of this method—one that breathes through the eight elements (dhātus) pervaded by breaths consisting of the doubled earth, water, fire, and air elements, which are contained within two layers and function as the sites of walking, standing, lying down, and sitting, indicated by [the corpses] such as those with headless trunks (*kabandha*), those hung up, those lying down, and those pierced by stakes—one should visualize the eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*).

Then, having visualized the two feet as the bow-shaped Vāyavya-maṇḍala, the surface of the navel as the triangular Āgneya-maṇḍala, the belly as the circular Vāruṇa-maṇḍala, and the chest as the square Māhendra-maṇḍala, one should visualize the head as the eight-peaked Sumeru mountain.

Then, upon that [crown], one should visualize the brain as a thirty-two-petaled lotus; in its center, a moon mandala; within that, the mouth of the central channel (nāḍī) shaped like a bird’s beak; there, the unstruck sound (*anāhata*) born from the vowels and consonants, the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is the very nature of Vajrasattva, the progenitor of the thirty-six channels. From that arises Śrī Heruka, who is innate (*sahaja*), resembling the moon, consisting of the Saṃbhogakāya, having Kālī as his intrinsic nature, appearing in the form of skillful means (*upāya*), whose essence is the perfectly pure wisdom of the Dharmadhātu, innate, and resembling the stainless sky.

One should resolve upon Vajravārāhī, who pervades all major and minor limbs and all directions of space, whose nature is the natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*), whose essence is the *āli* (vowels), who is the form of wisdom (*prajñā*), and whose nature is the utterly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātu*).

Then, within the *samayacakra*, at the lotus of the palate: on the eastern petal is the channel named Śaśī, which carries sound and is the eastern form of the Blessed One, having the nature of mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); she is Ḍākinī. On the northern petal is the channel named Kṣīravahā, which carries fragrance and is the northern form, having the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*); she is Lāmā. On the western petal is the channel named Snigdhā, which carries taste and is the western form, having the nature of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*); she is Khaṇḍarohā. On the southern petal is the channel named Madhurā, which carries touch and is the southern form, having the nature of all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

She is embodied (*rūpiṇī*). Others say she is in the heart-lotus; others declare she is in the four faces. On the corner petals are four channels (*praṇāḍikā*) that carry the *bodhicitta*, which are of the nature of worship and are skull-cups (*karoṭaka*) of *bodhicitta*. Thus, the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) is the stage of a Buddha, the armor of the vajra, the three principles (*tritatva*), the three worlds, and the three bodies (*trikāya*).
It consists of the place, the bed, and the nature of the wheel of commitment (*samayacakra*).

Then, one should meditate upon the seed-syllables—*pu*, *jā*, *o*, *a*, *go*, *rā*, *de*, *mā*, *kā*, *o*, *tri*, *ko*, *ka*, *laṃ*, *kāṃ*, *hi*, *pre*, *gṛ*, *sau*, *su*, *na*, *si*, *ma*, *ku*—in their respective locations in due order. Then, at Pullīramalaya on the head, there is the channel (*nāḍī*) Pracaṇḍā, which carries the nails, teeth, and wind (*vaha-aja*) of Khaṇḍakapālin. At Jālandhara on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), there is the channel Caṇḍākṣī, which carries the hair of Mahākaṅkāla and the fire (*vaha-hata*). At Oḍiyāna in the right ear, there is the channel Prabhāvatī, which carries the skin and impurities of Kaṅkāla (*vaha-mala*).

On the back of the head at Arbuda is Mahānāsā, the channel that carries the flesh of the fanged one and possesses strength. This is the *pīṭha*; she is Pramuditā; her gift is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*). At Godāvarī in the left ear is Vīramatī, the channel that carries the sinews of the enemy of the gods (Śiva). At Rāmeśvara between the eyebrows is Kharvarī, the channel that carries the bones of Amitābha. At Devikoṭa in the two eyes is Laṅkeśvarī, the channel that carries the palate of Vajraprabha.

In Mālava, at the two shoulders, is the *nāḍī* Drumacchāyā, which carries the heart of Vajradeha; this is the secondary seat (*upapīṭha*), [associated with] the *vimalā* stage, ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*). The mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) is Dharma, Hūṃ, Khecarī, Heaven, and Dissolution (*laya*). In Kāmarūpa, at the two armpits, is the *nāḍī* Airāvatī, which carries Aṅkurika and Akṣivahāmaha. In Oḍra, at the pair of breasts, is the *nāḍī* Mahābhairavā, which carries Vajrajaṭila and Pittavahāva; this is the field (*kṣetra*), [associated with] the *prabhākarī* stage, patience (*kṣānti*), and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).

In Triśakuni, at the navel, is the channel Vāyuvega, which carries the Mahāvīra-phupphusa; it is the Surābhakṣī. In Kosala, at the tip of the nose, is the channel Vajrahūṃkāra-antravahā-balā; it is the Śyāmādevī. Thus is the Upakṣetra, the Arciṣmatī bhūmi, Vīrya-pāramitā, and Mārgajñatā. In Kaliṅga, at the mouth, is the channel Subhadra-guṇavarti-vahā-madā; it is the Subhadrā. In Lampāka, at the throat, is the channel Subhadrodara-vahā-saukhyadā; it is the Subhadrā. Thus is the Chandoha, the Abhimukhī bhūmi, Dhyāna-pāramitā, and Kṣayajñāna.

In Kāñcī, at the heart, is the Hayakarṇā channel, which carries the thick excrement of Mahābhairava. In Himālaya, at the penis, is the Khagānanā channel, which is white and carries the parting of the hair of Virūpākṣa. Thus is the Upacchandoha; Sudurjayā is the wisdom of the non-arising of gnosis. This is the Wheel of Speech; ĀḤ is the enjoyment; Bhūcarī is the mortal experience. In Pretapurī, at the lingam, is the Cakravegā channel, which carries the great force of phlegm. In Gṛhadevatā, at the anus, is the Khaṇḍarohā channel, which carries the jewel-vajra and pus.

Thus, the meeting (*melāpaka*) is the far-reaching means (*dūraṅgamopāya*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). In Saurāṣṭra, in the two thighs, is the channel *Śauṇḍinī*, which carries the blood of Hayagrīva and is radiant. In Suvarṇadvīpa, in the shanks, is the channel *Cakravarmiṇī*, which carries the sweat of Ākāśagarbha and is tender. Thus, the near-meeting (*upamelāpaka*) is the immovable (*acalā*), the application (*praṇidhāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). In Nagara, in the fingers, is the channel *Suvīrā*, which carries the urine of Śrī Heruka and is firm. In Sindh, on the tops of the feet, is the channel *Mahābalā*, which carries the tears of Padmanarteśvara and is deceitful (*śaṭhā*).

Thus, the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) is Sādhumatī; power (*bala*) is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). In Maru, at the two thumbs, the channel (*nāḍī*) that carries Vairocana’s saliva is Cakravartinī. In Kulatā, at the knees, the channel that carries Vajrasattva’s lion’s roar is Mahāvīryā. Thus, the secondary cremation ground (*upaśmaśāna*) is Dharmameghā; gnosis (*jñāna*) is the knowledge of others’ minds (*paracittajñāna*). Thus is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), the emanation (*nirmāṇa*); *Oṃ*, Pātālavāsinī, and the underworld (*pātāla*) are the domain of authority. At the mouth-gate, the fierce channel is Kākāsyā.

At the right nostril is the channel Ghorā, Ulūkāsyā; at the anus is the channel Agnivadanā, Śvānāsyā; at the left nostril is the channel Tejinī, Sūkarāsyā; in the left ear is the channel Khaḍgadhāraṇī, Yamadāḍhī; in the right ear is the channel Cakrī, Yamadūtī; in the right eye is the channel Sūcīmukhā, Yamadaṃṣṭrī; and in the left eye is the channel Kubjī, Yamamathanī. Regarding this, some say as follows:

The channels situated at the left foot’s upper ankle, heel, and right ankle are the Gatekeepers (dvārapālī); those situated at the right foot’s tip, right ankle, heel, and left ankle are the Yoginīs dwelling in the corners (koṇavāsinī). In this way, one should meditate upon the mandala of the support and the supported within the body.
Oḍiyāna is in the right ear;
Subhadra, Guṇavarti, and Vahāmada (? are in the left ear.
If [she is] one of virtuous mind... [explicit]
